title: MA9-01802
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, Mr. XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, is a Mexican citizen. Mr XXXXX XXXXX is claiming to be a Convention refugee and a person in need of protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant stated that he was a victim of extortion by a group of thugs belonging to the Mexican mafia, la Mana.
The claimant was working at XXXXX when he received a call on XXXXX, 2008. The caller knew a great deal of personal information about the claimant.
On XXXXX, the same man called the claimant back and demanded $15,000. To show the claimant that they knew where he lived, they had cars drive around outside his home.
The claimant spoke to a colleague, XXXXX XXXXX, about the situation, and Mr. XXXXX told him that he was having the same problem.
The claimant left his job on XXXXX, 2008, because of the constant death threats he was receiving. Both the claimant and his colleague tried to come up with as much money as possible.

On XXXXX, while the claimant and his colleague were waiting for a bus, they were surrounded by four pickup trucks. The claimant and his colleague were kidnapped, beaten and threatened. They were ordered to deliver the money the next day at 4:00 p.m. They were taken to an isolated area where they were again beaten and threatened. Then, they were left there after being given instructions on when and where to leave the money being demanded. The claimant and his colleague hid at a friend's house. From there, they collected $5,000. The next day, XXXXX, they went to the location specified to deliver the money, as per the instructions they had been given.

They then fled the city of XXXXX and went to XXXXX, where they spent several days in a hotel. However, on XXXXX they decided to file a complaint, so they returned to XXXXX in order to do so. They then went back into hiding in XXXXX.
The claimant arrived in Canada on November 12, 2008, and claimed refugee protection that same day.
After analyzing the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel determines that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity

Given the documents submitted as evidence-namely, the photocopy of his passport, which is valid from XXXXX 2006, to XXXXX, 2011; and the photocopy of his voter's card, which was issued in 1999-the panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity. Credibility

The claimant's testimony was not credible because of omissions in the complaint document submitted and in the statements he made upon his arrival; he also made some statements in his testimony that were implausible and contradictory.

The panel first wanted to understand why the only document1 that the claimant submitted (he also submitted receipts from his company at the beginning of the hearing), namely the complaint he made to the police, contained a great deal of information about the threatening phone calls he had received and his kidnapping but did not make any mention of the $5,000 that he and his colleague claimed to have dropped off on XXXXX, 2008, the day after they were kidnapped. There was also no mention of the fact that they were thrown out of the vehicle in an isolated area and that, once they were out of the vehicle, they were again beaten, insulted and threatened with a revolver. When questioned on the subject, the claimant explained that he had provided this information to the police but that the police officer was arrogant and had not written it down.

The panel does not believe this explanation because the complaint was very detailed. For example, in its description of the kidnapping, it mentioned the location from which the claimant was kidnapped, the time at which the kidnapping occurred, the location where the claimant ended up, the types and colours of the vehicles, the thugs' actions and clothing, etc. The panel is of the opinion that the police had nothing to gain by failing to write down that the claimants had to pay $5,000 the day after the kidnapping, since the payment of this amount would constitute significant evidence of extortion. It would therefore have been reasonable for the claimant to mention the ransom to the police, which he did not do. The panel therefore does not believe that the ransom was actually paid, which undermines the claimant's credibility.

In addition, when the claimant was interviewed by an immigration officer2 upon his arrival in Canada, he made no mention of the alleged kidnapping or ransom. At most, he stated that he had received telephone calls with extortion demands. When questioned on this subject, he stated that he had nevertheless explained it and that he had given his complaint document to the police at that time; he also provided some vague explanations about a possible translation problem.

The panel does not believe that the claimant made a statement to the effect that he was kidnapped even though he submitted his complaint document. The space provided for this answer is only one line since usually only a short response is required, and yet the immigration officer wrote over 13 lines on the back of the page in order to document what the claimant had said. It is therefore reasonable to assume that, if information about a kidnapping was provided, it also would have been documented, which was not the case. In addition, there was no mention of an interpreter in this document. Had the services of an interpreter been used, the panel does not see what benefit he or she would have derived from failing to interpret such a key point.

As a result, although the claimant seemed emotional when he described the kidnapping, the panel does not believe that it actually occurred, at least not after he received the extortion threats, as the claimant described; the claimant did not mention the kidnapping upon his arrival in Canada, whereas he did provide a fair bit of information about the telephone calls he had received.

Furthermore, the panel finds it unlikely that, when they called the claimant to threaten him, the kidnappers did not provide him with any information about where, when and how the ransom should be delivered. When questioned in this regard, the claimant stated that it was only once he was kidnapped that he was told that he should drop the ransom off the next day at a specific location. The panel finds this implausible because, if the claimant had been asked for money many times or almost every day from XXXXX to XXXXX as he alleged at the hearing, it would be reasonable to expect that those demanding the ransom would tell him when and where he should drop off the money demanded. The panel questioned the claimant on this subject twice, but he maintained that nothing had been said about this until he was kidnapped. This implausibility undermines the claimant's credibility, even more so because it is surprising that four vehicles and about ten people would come surround the claimant and his colleague and kidnap them on XXXXX when the kidnappers had not yet given them any specific instructions on how the ransom was to be paid.

The panel also wanted to understand why the claimant in particular was receiving threatening calls with extortion demands, since he stated that he had been earning the equivalent of only $100 per week; he submitted pay stubs from his company to support this statement.3 In response to a question from his counsel, he explained that the reason could be that he often crossed the border. His town, XXXXX, which is located in the state of Tamaulipas, is about 25 minutes from the border. He was responsible for quality control at XXXXX Controls, which manufactures automobile valves. He went to the United States two or three times per week because he was responsible for labelling the equipment sent there. The panel pointed out to him that there is no indication on his passport,4 which he has had since XXXXX 2006, that he crossed the American border. The claimant explained that he crossed the border with an electronic card or visa. He would be asked for his passport and the electronic card, and it was the card that was swiped through the reader because he travelled frequently.

Later in the hearing, the claimant stated that, when he was kidnapped, the kidnappers took his bag and all his documents, which included his electronic card, his military card, his unique population registry code (CURP)5 card and his social insurance card. They therefore had access to all his personal information. The panel asked him why he still had his voter's card-one of his ID cards-and he explained that he still had it because he does not usually carry it with him.

In response to other questions asked by the panel later in the hearing, the claimant said that he could not take refuge elsewhere in Mexico because these thugs had too much information about him and could easily find him. The panel noted that his passport was not stolen, since he had it with him when he arrived in Canada, yet the claimant said that he needed his passport to cross the border, which meant that he must have had to have it with him often since he had to cross the border two or three times per week. The claimant then tried to adjust his testimony by stating that he was asked for the electronic card and his company card. When the panel pointed out to him that he had stated earlier that he had to show his passport and his electronic card, he said that this was true when he had to travel within the United States but, when he was crossing the border for work, he showed only his company card and the electronic card and that a call would sometimes be made to verify that he did indeed work for the company in question.

The panel does not believe these explanations because the claimant clearly stated earlier that he had to show his passport and his electronic card when he crossed the border. The panel finds that the claimant could not have had all his documents stolen as he claimed. This contradiction undermines his credibility and lends little credibility to his fear of establishing himself elsewhere in Mexico.
For all of these reasons, the panel finds that the claimant is not credible.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel determines that the claimant did not prove that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds should he return to Mexico. He also failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to Mexico.

Consequently, his claim for refugee protection is rejected.
